title: The Power of Music
author: Sukumar Ray
tagline: A singer whose voice flattens the countryside — until a sagacious billy goat answers him in his own coin.

sourceNote.thirdParty: "The Power of Music" is a nonsense poem by Sukumar Ray (Bengali original in Abol Tabol, 1923), translated into English by Sukanta Chaudhuri, and remains the property of its copyright holders. The poem is not reproduced here. Read it in your prescribed textbook.
sourceNote.boardprep: The summary, device and theme notes, vocabulary and all questions and answers on this page were written by BoardPrep as original study material and are not taken from any textbook or guide.

overview.intro: Sukumar Ray's comic nonsense verse introduces Bhisma Lochan Sharma, a singer of such tremendous volume that his music sweeps from Delhi towards Burma, overturning carts, distressing animals and drowning every protest. The poem's joke is drawn out patiently: everyone suffers, nobody can stop him, and it takes one well-aimed billy goat to restore the silence that the whole poem has been arguing for. Read it as a performance piece — the exaggeration, the lists of havoc and the rhyming rollick are all built to be read aloud.

learn.title: Before you read: nonsense verse and its rules

blocks.text: Nonsense verse is a serious comic tradition: it exaggerates the world until logic squeaks, yet its jokes are precisely engineered. Edward Lear is its English-language grandfather, and Sukumar Ray is its Bengali master — a poet, songwriter and illustrator whose short poems turn ordinary situations into gloriously unstoppable disasters. In this poem the ordinary situation is a man singing loudly; the disaster is everything else.

As you read aloud, notice that the comedy comes in lists: the poem keeps expanding its catalogue of damage — carts, horses, fish, trees, birds — so that each line adds another victim. Also track the people's pleas, which repeat without effect. The poem is really an argument in verse: what happens when 'power' (here, music) stops listening to anyone?

The poem opens on its hero, Bhisma Lochan Sharma, whose singing is stupendously loud and carries across an enormous imagined landscape, from Delhi towards Burma. Wherever the sound reaches, it causes comic havoc: bullock carts topple, horses are terrified, fish plunge to the lake bed hoping for quiet, trees shake, and birds are knocked upside down in mid-air. The people beg him, politely and then desperately, to stop — but he sings on, oblivious, apparently convinced of his own magnificence.

items: The singer's voice establishes its range first: the poem's boast is geographical.
A catalogue of destruction follows — carts, animals, trees and birds all fall victim to the noise.
The people's repeated pleas are reported in direct speech, and each one changes nothing.
At the climax a 'sagacious' billy goat charges the singer and answers his bellow with a bellow of his own.
The singing stops. The poem closes by savouring the silence that follows as something precious.
The victory belongs to the least musical character in the poem — which is the joke's final twist.

items.text: The havoc is presented as a running list of nature and everyday life disrupted.
items.note: The catalogue form is itself a nonsense technique: each new victim funnily tops the last.

items.text: The people plead repeatedly, but only the goat acts.
items.note: The poem satirises helpless, polite audiences — words do nothing; one decisive deed ends it.

blocks.text: Bhisma Lochan Sharma is the self-important artist as disaster. He is never described as malicious — merely unstoppable and unconcerned, which is Ray's satire on performers who love their own volume and never check whether anyone is enjoying it. His name, grand and archaic, adds to the comedy: the magnificent title belongs to a man whose singing flattens fish. He does not change or learn during the poem; he simply gets shut down.

The people and animals form the suffering chorus — their function is to show the reach of the noise and the futility of asking nicely. Into this helpless world steps the billy goat, whom the poem ironically labels sagacious: wisdom here consists of doing the obvious thing nobody dared. The goat does not out-sing the singer; he simply matches volume with volume, and the poem's logic — a nonsense world governed by noise — makes that the perfect reply.

items.meaning: The thunderous, oblivious singer whose performance causes havoc across the land.
The 'sagacious' animal whose answering bellow finally silences the song.
The pleading, powerless audience who ask the singer to stop and are ignored.
Comic poetry that exaggerates reality with precise linguistic play and a mock-serious tone.
Extreme exaggeration not meant literally — the poem's basic fuel.

blocks.text: The poem imitates its subject: the lines rush, tumble and pile up like the singer's noise. Hyperbole does the heaviest work — a voice crossing from Delhi towards Burma, fish diving for peace, birds flipped upside down — every image tops the last because nonsense logic allows no ceiling. Repetition gives the people's pleas their comic futility: each request is answered by more singing, so repetition becomes the poem's evidence that politeness is useless here.

items: Read the poem aloud twice: its comedy is acoustic before it is intellectual.
The images escalate in scale — ground (carts), animals, water (fish), then sky (birds).
The goat's reply mirrors the singer's own weapon: noise defeated by noise.

blocks.text: The poem's first theme is the misuse of art: music becomes power when the performer stops listening. Bhisma Lochan Sharma sings for himself; the audience exists only as an obstacle to more sound. Ray satirises the artist who confuses intensity with excellence and volume with talent — a joke that travels easily to any performer, speaker or institution that drowns out its hearers. The people's helpless pleading is the poem's sharper edge: self-absorption is dangerous not least because everyone else is too polite to stop it.

Beneath the nonsense runs a celebration of silence. The poem's closing movement — savouring the quiet after the goat's intervention — reveals what the whole catalogue of havoc has been arguing: quiet is not emptiness but a gift, easily lost and quickly missed. The final reversal carries the moral without stating one: the most effective character is an animal with no musical pretension at all, and the solution arrives when someone finally does the simple thing everyone else only requested.

items: Art versus noise: intensity and volume are not the same as merit.
Self-absorption: the singer never notices or cares about his effect on others.
The power — and weakness — of audiences: pleading without acting changes nothing.
The value of silence: quiet is the poem's hidden treasure, revealed only when it returns.
Decisive action: the goat succeeds because he acts where everyone else only spoke.

learn.title: Reading and writing tips for this poem

blocks.text: Nonsense poems are examined on technique and meaning together: name the device (hyperbole, catalogue, repetition), cite the shape of an example rather than quoting at length, and then explain the effect — usually comedy plus satire. The ending is the classic question: be ready to explain why the goat is called sagacious, why noise defeats noise, and what the restored silence signifies. Practise reading a stanza aloud first; answers about rhythm sound far better from students who have heard it.

items: For 'describe the havoc', use the catalogue structure of the poem itself — ground, animals, water, sky.
For a satire question, contrast the singer's grandeur with his obliviousness.
For a theme question, pair 'excessive sound' with 'the value of silence'; they are one argument.
Avoid invented quotations: paraphrase the incidents precisely and keep the poem's sequence.

keyPoints: The poem is a nonsense verse narrative: Bhisma Lochan Sharma's singing causes havoc until a goat stops it.
Hyperbole drives the comedy — a voice described as sweeping from Delhi towards Burma.
The catalogue of damage (carts, horses, fish, trees, birds) escalates so each victim outdoes the last.
The people's repeated, ineffective pleas satirise polite audiences who never act.
The goat is ironically called sagacious: wisdom here means doing the obvious thing decisively.
Sound defeats noise: the goat answers the singer with the singer's own weapon.
The closing silence is celebrated as something precious — the poem's quiet moral.
Themes: self-absorbed art, the misuse of power, the weakness of pleading, and the value of quiet.
Techniques to name in answers: hyperbole, catalogue, repetition, rhyming play, mock-heroic tone and irony.
examFocus: Narrative question: give the poem's sequence — fame and range, catalogue of havoc, pleas, the goat, silence — in order.
Devices question: name hyperbole and catalogue first, illustrate their shape, then explain the comic effect.
Character: the singer = grandiose and oblivious; the goat = ironic wisdom; the people = helpless politeness.
The ending is the favourite target: be ready to explain 'sagacious', the mirroring of bellow by bellow, and the restored silence.
Satire answer: the poem targets performers who love their own output more than their audience.

vocabulary.meaning: Comic poetry that exaggerates and distorts the world for playful effect.
vocabulary.context: Sukumar Ray is a master of nonsense verse, and this poem is one of his best-known pieces.

vocabulary.meaning: Deliberate extreme exaggeration, not meant to be believed literally.
vocabulary.context: The song's reach from Delhi towards Burma is hyperbole announcing the voice's comic power.

vocabulary.meaning: A list of items presented one after another.
vocabulary.context: The poem's catalogue of victims — carts, horses, fish, trees, birds — builds the havoc line by line.

vocabulary.meaning: Completely unaware of what is happening around one.
vocabulary.context: The singer carries on, oblivious to the pleading and the damage.

vocabulary.meaning: Very wise or shrewd — here used ironically and affectionately.
vocabulary.context: The billy goat is called sagacious because charging the singer is the one wise, decisive act.

vocabulary.meaning: Humour used to expose and criticise faults or follies.
vocabulary.context: The poem satirises self-absorbed performers and audiences that only plead.
The goat answers the singer's bellow with a bellow — noise matched by noise.

vocabulary.meaning: Treating a trivial or ridiculous subject with the seriousness of epic poetry.
vocabulary.context: The grand treatment of a mere loud singer is mock-heroic and part of the satire.

questions.prompt: How does the poem finally silence Bhisma Lochan Sharma?
options: The people persuade him to stop by begging more sincerely
A sagacious billy goat charges him and answers his bellow with a bellow of his own
He sings himself hoarse and cannot continue
A storm blows up and carries the sound away
questions.answer: A sagacious billy goat charges him and answers his bellow with a bellow of his own
questions.explanation: All the people's polite pleading fails; only the goat's matching noise works. The poem's logic is that the singer can only be defeated on his own terms — by a sound at least as determined as his own.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing that the people succeed — their pleas are reported as useless throughout; the reversal depends on that failure.

questions.prompt: What is the best description of the singer in the poem?
options: A cruel man who deliberately torments his neighbours
A modest artist who is embarrassed by his own fame
A grandiose, oblivious performer who never notices the havoc he causes
A shy singer who needs encouragement before he will begin
questions.answer: A grandiose, oblivious performer who never notices the havoc he causes
questions.explanation: Ray's satire needs a singer who is not evil but indifferent: convinced of his own magnificence, he sings through carts overturning and people pleading. The comedy and the criticism both depend on his obliviousness.
questions.commonMistake: Calling him deliberately cruel — the poem's point is that self-absorbed performers do not notice, not that they intend harm.

questions.prompt: Describe the havoc caused by the singer's voice, in the order the poem presents it.
questions.answer: The voice sweeps across the countryside and its damage is catalogued: bullock carts overturn on the roads, horses are distressed, fish dive to the bottom of the lake in search of quiet, trees shake, and birds are knocked topsy-turvy in flight. The list climbs from the ground upwards — carts, animals, water, sky — until every part of the landscape is suffering from the noise.
questions.explanation: The description should preserve the catalogue structure and its upward scale, which is the joke's design: each new victim funnily outdoes the previous one.
questions.commonMistake: Listing incidents in random order — the escalating arrangement is part of the poem's technique.

questions.prompt: How do the people try to stop the singing, and why does their effort fail?
questions.answer: The people plead with the singer, their requests reported in direct speech and repeated as the havoc grows — first politely, then more desperately. Their effort fails because the singer simply does not listen: he is absorbed in his own performance, and words aimed at him bounce off. The poem implies that polite audiences can protest endlessly without ever changing anything.
questions.explanation: Two parts are needed: what they do (repeated pleas in direct speech) and why it fails (his obliviousness, and the futility of words without action).
questions.commonMistake: Saying the people give up — the poem's force comes from pleading that continues and still achieves nothing.

questions.prompt: How does Sukumar Ray use exaggeration to create comedy in this poem? Illustrate your answer.
questions.answer: Ray's basic comic tool is hyperbole: the singer's voice is described as carrying from Delhi towards Burma, turning volume into geography, and each image of damage outdoes the last — carts overturn, fish dive for peace, trees shake, birds tumble in the air. The exaggeration is organised as a catalogue, so the comedy accumulates rather than peaks: the reader is invited to guess what will be wrecked next. Scale is also set against dignity: the singer bears a grand, archaic name while flattening fish and poultry, and mock-heroic treatment of a mere noise-maker is the poem's satire of self-importance. The result is comedy with a target — every absurd image is also an argument about performers who never check their effect on listeners.
questions.explanation: Name the device (hyperbole), show its structure (escalating catalogue), add the tone (mock-heroic), and connect to effect (comedy carrying satire). Illustrations may describe rather than quote.
questions.commonMistake: Only listing funny images — the answer must explain how the exaggeration is organised and what it criticises.

questions.prompt: What does the poem suggest about audiences who only plead? Use the people's responses in your answer.
questions.answer: The people do the respectable thing: they ask, they explain, they repeat themselves — and nothing changes. Ray makes their pleas a running refrain precisely so their futility becomes comic and then pointed: an audience that only uses words gives a self-absorbed performer an unlimited licence. The turning point of the poem is that success comes from someone who does not plead at all — the goat acts. The poem therefore praises decisiveness over politeness, while quietly warning that every community gets the silence it is willing to fight for. The people are not villains; they are simply the ordinary condition the poem is satirising.
questions.explanation: The answer must move from evidence (repeated, ignored pleas) to inference (pleading without action empowers the offender) to judgement (the poem values action), using the goat as contrast.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the people as foolish or evil — the satire is on the habit of pleading, not on their characters.

questions.prompt: Why is the goat called 'sagacious'? Explain the irony and the logic of his intervention.
questions.answer: Sagacious means profoundly wise, and applying it to a goat that simply head-butts a singer is affectionate irony — Ray elevates an animal act to a statesman's decision. Yet within the poem's nonsense logic the description is exact: everyone else can see what should be done, and only the goat does it, so wisdom here is the courage to act on the obvious. The method also fits the world Ray has built: in a poem where everything runs on noise, the correct counter to an unbearable sound is a louder, unanswerable one — the goat answers bellow with bellow. Wisdom, the poem jokes, is sometimes just matching the bully on his own terms and restoring the quiet nobody else would fight for.
questions.explanation: Full marks need three layers: the literal meaning of the word, the ironic application to an animal, and the in-world logic (obvious action; noise answered by noise) that makes the irony double as praise.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining only the dictionary meaning — the question asks for the irony AND the logic.

questions.prompt: What is the poem's final judgement on the silence after the singing stops?
questions.answer: The poem closes by treasuring the restored silence — presenting quiet not as absence but as a gift worth having. After pages of escalating noise, the sudden quiet is the real prize, and the ending lets the reader feel how precious ordinary quiet is once a community has been made to lose it.
questions.explanation: The closing celebration of silence is the poem's quiet moral: sound was treated as power throughout, and only when it ends does the value of quiet become visible.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the poem ends with the goat's triumph alone — the LAST note is on silence, which is the concluding judgement.

questions.prompt: 'The poem argues that art becomes tyranny when no one can stop it.' Discuss this reading with reference to the singer and the goat.
questions.answer: For the reading: the singer's music begins as art and becomes a force of destruction precisely because it is unstoppable — carts, animals, trees and birds suffer while he sings on, delighted. His obliviousness is the tyrant's signature: the audience exists only as an obstacle, and its pleas are beneath notice. In this light the goat is liberator as well as comedian: he ends a tyranny not by debating it but by matching it, and the celebrated silence that follows is freedom restored. Against the reading: the poem never lets the singer intend harm — he is ridiculous rather than wicked, and the havoc is nonsense exaggeration, not a treatise on art's politics; tyranny suggests deliberate oppression, whereas this singer simply does not think about anyone. The stronger judgement holds both: Ray teases the grandiose performer who mistakes volume for value, and the poem's joke contains a real warning — art that cannot be interrupted stops being art for its listeners and becomes merely noise they must endure. The goat, fittingly, is the listener who finally answers back.
questions.explanation: A discuss response must argue both sides — evidence for (unstoppable havoc, ignored pleas, restored silence) and objection (nonsense comic register, no evil intent) — before committing to a balanced verdict anchored in both singer and goat.
questions.commonMistake: Taking the reading as literal plot summary — the marks lie in weighing whether a comic nonsense poem really carries that political weight.

questions.prompt: If the goat had not arrived, how would the poem have had to end? Write the continuation you think the poem's own logic demands, and justify your choices.
questions.answer: The poem's logic demands an ending in which noise is defeated by noise, because Ray's world runs on volume and his satire depends on interruption rather than persuasion. Without the goat, the people's pleading would escalate further — petitions, delegations, ever-politer requests — and the singer, oblivious as ever, would simply sing louder, until the catalogue of havoc reached its ridiculous ceiling (ships confused at sea, birds nesting in panic, whole towns clapping their ears). The only fitting rescue would then come from some other unlettered, unimpressed creature — a donkey, a flock of geese, a thunderstorm that out-bellows him — because the poem has already taught us that conversations with the self-absorbed achieve nothing. Whatever the rescuer, two features are obligatory: it must answer sound with sound, and it must end on silence savoured as a gift. The goat works because he is simplest and funniest; any replacement must keep that shape.
questions.explanation: This creative-response question is marked on fidelity to the poem's method: escalation of the catalogue, failure of pleading, noise answered by noise, silence treasured at the close — plus a justified choice of rescuer.
questions.commonMistake: Ending with the people successfully persuading him — that contradicts the poem's entire argument about pleading.
